claim: PLISH generates signals that exceed cellular and tissue fluorescence background by more than 30-fold.
source: The signal from the individual RCA amplicons exceeded cellular and tissue fluorescence background by more than 30-fold, rendering autofluorescence inconsequential (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A–B and [Jarvius et al., 2006; Blab et al., 2004]).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplements 1A–B showing background measurements and by citations to prior work

claim: Histograms of PLISH puncta intensities fit to a negative binomial distribution.
source: Histograms of puncta intensities fit to a negative binomial distribution, as expected for a DNA replication process that terminates stochastically and irreversibly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F and by inference about DNA replication processes

claim: The coefficients of variation for PLISH puncta intensity distributions were typically between one and two.
source: The coefficients of variation for the puncta intensity distributions were typically between one and two.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data

claim: A pool of ten H probesets exhibited much higher RNA detection efficiency than a single H probeset.
source: A pool of ten H probesets exhibited much higher RNA detection efficiency than a single H probeset, as expected (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: When the RNA-recognition sequence of either the left or right H probe in each set was scrambled, there were no detectable puncta.
source: However, when the RNA-recognition sequence of either the left or right H probe in each set was scrambled, there were no detectable puncta.
evidence: Directly stated experimental observation

claim: Both H probes must be correctly targeted to generate a PLISH signal.
source: Thus, both H probes had to be correctly targeted to generate a signal.
evidence: Inferred from the scrambled probe experiment results

claim: Antisense oligonucleotides drastically attenuated the number of PLISH puncta for Scgb1a1.
source: Antisense oligonucleotides drastically attenuated the number of PLISH puncta, whereas scrambled blocking oligonucleotides of the same length had no apparent effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E

claim: 98.5% of cells positive for PLISH signal for Sftpc were also positive for antibody staining.
source: Of the cells that were positive for PLISH signal, 98.5% were also positive for antibody staining (n = 184, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from co-localization experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: PLISH specificity is excellent relative to HCR-amplified smISH, where off-target binding can account for a quarter of observed puncta.
source: This level of specificity is excellent relative to HCR-amplified smISH, where off-target binding of hybridization probes can account for a quarter of the observed puncta (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: Comparison to published data on HCR-amplified smISH

claim: For genes with FPKM values greater than one, single-cell qPCR detected mRNA in >90% of cells.
source: For genes with fragment-per-kilobase-per-million-read (FPKM) values greater than one, the single-cell qPCR technique detected mRNA in >90% of the cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by reference dataset from Wu et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 1F

claim: An FPKM value of one corresponds to 2.5 copies per cell.
source: A fit of the qPCR data to a Poisson sampling model suggested that an FPKM value of one corresponded to 2.5 copies per cell (see also [Marinov et al., 2014; Battich et al., 2013]).
evidence: Derived from fitting qPCR data to a Poisson model, supported by citations

claim: PLISH detects RNA transcripts with a sensitivity comparable to single-cell qPCR.
source: The PLISH technique detected RNA transcripts with a sensitivity comparable to single-cell qPCR.
evidence: Comparison of PLISH data to qPCR reference data

claim: CASP9 has an FPKM value of 2 and was observed in 100% of cells by PLISH.
source: For example, Caspase-9 (CASP9) has an FPKM value of 2, and it was observed in 100% of the cells by PLISH.
evidence: Direct measurement from PLISH experiment

claim: PLISH detected an average of 8 puncta per cell for CASP9.
source: We detected an average of 8 puncta per cell, which is consistent with the prediction of 5 copies per cell from the fit to the qPCR data (Figure 1F, inset).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PLISH experiment shown in Figure 1F inset

claim: For ten genes covering the full spectrum of expression levels in HCT116 cells, the number of PLISH puncta per cell correlated with bulk FPKM values.
source: For a set of ten genes covering the full spectrum of expression levels in HCT116 cells, the number of PLISH puncta per cell correlated with bulk FPKM values (Figure 1G).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G

claim: Four PLISH probesets detected Axin2 transcripts with a composite efficiency of 32%.
source: Thus, the four PLISH probesets detected Axin2 transcripts with a composite efficiency of 32% and an average per-site efficiency of 9%.
evidence: Calculated from co-localization experiment with HCR

claim: PLISH has an average per-site detection efficiency of 9% for Axin2.
source: Thus, the four PLISH probesets detected Axin2 transcripts with a composite efficiency of 32% and an average per-site efficiency of 9%.
evidence: Calculated from co-localization experiment with HCR

claim: PLISH detection efficiency matches or exceeds that of other smISH techniques.
source: This probe efficiency matches or exceeds that of other smISH techniques.
evidence: Comparison to other techniques based on established knowledge

claim: PLISH detection efficiency can be tuned on a per gene basis by altering the number of H probe pairs.
source: The PLISH detection efficiency can be tuned on a per gene basis by altering the number of H probe pairs.
evidence: Stated as a property of the technique

claim: PLISH provides single-molecule resolution in tissues.
source: We aimed to test whether PLISH provides single-molecule and single-cell resolution in tissues, whether it robustly detects low-abundance RNA species, whether the spatial distribution of RNA is consistent with prior knowledge, whether PLISH is compatible with simultaneous immunostaining, and whether it is compatible with formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples.
evidence: Demonstrated by observation of discrete Foxj1 puncta in Figure 2B

claim: PLISH provides single-cell resolution in tissues.
source: These data establish PLISH's single-molecule and single-cell resolution in tissues, and its ability to detect low-abundance transcripts.
evidence: Demonstrated by observation of single ciliated cells in Figure 2B

claim: Foxj1 is a low-abundance transcript with an FPKM value of 10 in ciliated cells.
source: Foxj1 is a low-abundance transcript with an FPKM value of 10 in ciliated cells, as measured by scRNA-seq (Treutlein et al., 2014).
evidence: Referenced from published scRNA-seq data

claim: PLISH is compatible with simultaneous immunostaining.
source: These data establish PLISH's compatibility with simultaneous immunostaining, and with FFPE samples.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-staining for SCGB1A1 RNA and KRT5 protein in Figure 2C

claim: PLISH is compatible with FFPE samples.
source: These data establish PLISH's compatibility with simultaneous immunostaining, and with FFPE samples.
evidence: Demonstrated by successful staining of FFPE human lung in Figure 2C

claim: SCGB1A1 positive cells localize to the lumen of airways, overlying KRT5 positive cells.
source: Strongly SCGB1A1 positive cells were localized to the lumen of the airways, overlying KRT5 positive cells (Figure 2C), matching the known anatomical distribution of Club and basal cells, respectively.
evidence: Observed in Figure 2C and consistent with known anatomy

claim: The spatial distribution of SCGB1A1 and KRT5 matches the known anatomical distribution of Club and basal cells.
source: Strongly SCGB1A1 positive cells were localized to the lumen of the airways, overlying KRT5 positive cells (Figure 2C), matching the known anatomical distribution of Club and basal cells, respectively.
evidence: Comparison to established anatomical knowledge

claim: Macrophages are bright in the Lyz2 channel but absent in the Sftpc and Scgb1a1 channels.
source: Macrophages were bright in the Lyz2 channel, but absent in the other channels (Figure 2D).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2D

claim: AT2 cells are bright in the Sftpc channel, moderately bright in the Lyz2 channel, and absent in the Scgb1a1 channel.
source: AT2 cells were bright in the Sftpc channel, moderately bright in the Lyz2 channel and absent in the Scgb1a1 channel (Figure 2D, white cells in the overlay).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2D

claim: Club cells are very bright in the Scgb1a1 channel but otherwise absent.
source: Club cells were very bright in the Scgb1a1 channel, but otherwise absent (Figure 2E).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2E

claim: Putative BASCs are bright in the Sftpc channel with a weak punctate signal in the Scgb1a1 channel.
source: Finally, putative bronchioalveolar stem cells (Kim et al., 2005) (BASCs) were bright in the Sftpc channel with a weak punctate signal in the Scgb1a1 channel (Figure 2E).
evidence: Observed in Figure 2E and referenced to prior work on BASCs

claim: Raw PLISH data can be interpreted without any computational processing due to exceptional signal-to-noise in tissues.
source: Thus, raw PLISH data can be interpreted without any computational processing, made possible by PLISH's exceptional signal-to-noise in tissues.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to visually distinguish cell types in Figures 2D-E

claim: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal lung disease of unknown pathogenesis.
source: One example is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a fatal lung disease of unknown pathogenesis (Travis et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Travis et al., 2013

claim: The diagnosis of IPF is based on the presence of specific histological features, including clusters of spindle-shaped fibroblasts, stereotyped 'honeycomb' cysts, and epithelial cell hyperplasia.
source: The diagnosis of IPF is based on the presence of specific histological features, including clusters of spindle-shaped fibroblasts, stereotyped 'honeycomb' cysts, and epithelial cell hyperplasia.
evidence: Established medical knowledge about IPF diagnosis

claim: Single-cell profiling approaches that operate on dissociated tissue cannot correlate molecular data with cytologic and spatial features.
source: In this regard, single-cell profiling approaches that operate on dissociated tissue (Xu et al., 2016) are intrinsically limited because they cannot correlate molecular data with cytologic and spatial features.
evidence: Logical inference about limitations of dissociation-based methods

claim: In non-IPF lungs, SFTPC-expressing AT2 cells are uniformly cuboidal and distributed throughout alveoli.
source: In contrast to the uniformly cuboidal SFTPC-expressing AT2 cells distributed throughout alveoli of non-IPF lungs (Figure 2F), we observed clusters of SFTPCHi cells of heterogeneous size and varying degrees of flattening lining the airspace lumen of IPF lungs.
evidence: Observed in Figure 2F

claim: In IPF lungs, clusters of SFTPCHi cells of heterogeneous size and varying degrees of flattening line the airspace lumen.
source: In contrast to the uniformly cuboidal SFTPC-expressing AT2 cells distributed throughout alveoli of non-IPF lungs (Figure 2F), we observed clusters of SFTPCHi cells of heterogeneous size and varying degrees of flattening lining the airspace lumen of IPF lungs.
evidence: Observed in Figure 2F

claim: Many cells in IPF lungs that did not appear to be epithelial expressed SFTPC at low levels.
source: Surprisingly, many cells that did not appear to be epithelial (i.e., they were not lining an airway lumen) expressed SFTPC at low levels.
evidence: Observed in IPF tissue analysis

claim: PLISH should be a suitable tool for building atlases of RNA expression in human disease.
source: Based on this pilot experiment, PLISH should be a suitable tool for building atlases of RNA expression in human disease.
evidence: Inferred from successful application to IPF tissue

claim: PLISH puncta can be imaged in the presence of a 3 nM background of freely-diffusing imager oligonucleotides.
source: Consistent with prior work, we found that PLISH puncta could be imaged in the presence of a 3 nM background of freely-diffusing imager oligonucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplements 1A and [Blab et al., 2004]).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and consistent with cited prior work

claim: Fluorescence from PLISH puncta can be erased by a simple buffer exchange using short imager oligonucleotides that equilibrate rapidly on and off of RCA amplicons.
source: By using short imager oligonucleotides that equilibrate rapidly on and off of RCA amplicons (Jungmann et al., 2014), we could erase fluorescence from a previous cycle by a simple buffer exchange (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and referenced to prior work

claim: An erasure method based on uracil-containing imager oligonucleotides can be accomplished with a 15 min enzymatic digestion.
source: We also established an erasure method based on uracil-containing imager oligonucleotides, which were removed with a 15 min enzymatic digestion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: PLISH label-image-erase cycles can be completed in as little as 20 min.
source: Thus, we could image PLISH puncta in five different color channels with spectrally-distinct fluorophores, and we were able to complete cycles in as little as 20 min, which approaches the cycle time of an Illumina MiSeq instrument (https://support.illumina.com).
evidence: Directly stated measurement of cycle time

claim: The PLISH cycle time approaches the cycle time of an Illumina MiSeq instrument.
source: Thus, we could image PLISH puncta in five different color channels with spectrally-distinct fluorophores, and we were able to complete cycles in as little as 20 min, which approaches the cycle time of an Illumina MiSeq instrument (https://support.illumina.com).
evidence: Comparison to known sequencing instrument cycle time

claim: Eight different transcripts in mouse lung were visualized with two label-image-erase cycles.
source: To demonstrate and validate the multiplexing capacity of PLISH, we co-localized the mRNA of eight selected genes in ~2900 single cells from an adult mouse lung (Figure 3B).
evidence: Described experimental design and shown in Figure 3B

claim: The multiplexed PLISH experiment analyzed ~2900 single cells from adult mouse lung.
source: To demonstrate and validate the multiplexing capacity of PLISH, we co-localized the mRNA of eight selected genes in ~2900 single cells from an adult mouse lung (Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly stated sample size

claim: The bulk of detected mRNAs in AT1 cells were clustered around the nuclei.
source: Fortuitously, the bulk of the detected mRNAs in AT1 cells, which have an extremely flat and broad morphology, were clustered around the nuclei.
evidence: Observed during data analysis

claim: Automated and unsupervised analysis of multiplexed PLISH data identified ten cell classes.
source: The automated analysis identified ten cell classes, four of which were labeled 'other' because they were defined primarily by 'signature' profiles of ubiquitously-expressed genes.
evidence: Result of k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Six of the ten identified cell classes were associated with a known lung cell type based on marker-gene expression.
source: The remaining six classes were associated with a known lung cell type based on marker-gene expression.
evidence: Result of clustering analysis and marker gene interpretation

claim: One of the two AT2 cell classes is Lyz2 positive.
source: The Sftpc and Scgb1a1 positive cell classes were labeled as AT2 and Club, respectively, while the Lyz2 positive class was labeled as macrophage (one of the two AT2 cell classes was also Lyz2 positive as previously reported in (Desai et al., 2014), Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in clustering analysis and validated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, consistent with prior publication

claim: Ager mRNA is not particularly specific for AT1 cells.
source: The cell class with the highest Ager expression was labeled as AT1, but Ager mRNA was also detected in a subset of AT2 and Club cells, and in one of the four 'other' cell classes, indicating it is not particularly specific for AT1 cells.
evidence: Observed in PLISH data analysis

claim: Indirect immunohistochemistry and scRNA-seq data confirmed the low specificity of Ager for AT1 cells.
source: We validated the PLISH results by indirect immunohistochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and by comparison with previously published scRNA-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), which confirmed the low specificity of Ager for AT1 cells.
evidence: Validated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and scRNA-seq comparison in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Akap5 RNA expression localization correlates closely with Ager's.
source: We also analyzed the RNA expression of Akap5, another transcript that is highly-enriched in AT1 cells (Treutlein et al., 2014), and found that its localization correlated closely with Ager's (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Observed in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and referenced to prior work

claim: A small cloud of cells between the Club and AT2 clusters expressed both Sftpc and Scgb1a1.
source: We found a small cloud of cells between the Club and AT2 clusters that expressed both Sftpc and Scgb1a1.
evidence: Observed in t-SNE analysis

claim: Cells expressing both Sftpc and Scgb1a1 were assigned as the BASC type.
source: On the basis of this dual expression, we assigned them as the BASC type (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: Inferred from dual marker expression and referenced to prior work on BASCs

claim: Lyz2 expression partitions AT2 cells into two classes designated Lyz2+ and Lyz2-.
source: We also noted that Lyz2 expression partitioned the AT2 cells into two classes designated Lyz2+ and Lyz2-, while Actb segregated Club cells into two classes designated ActbHi and ActbLo.
evidence: Observed in t-SNE analysis

claim: Actb expression segregates Club cells into two classes designated ActbHi and ActbLo.
source: We also noted that Lyz2 expression partitioned the AT2 cells into two classes designated Lyz2+ and Lyz2-, while Actb segregated Club cells into two classes designated ActbHi and ActbLo.
evidence: Observed in t-SNE analysis

claim: Gapdh is the most uniformly expressed transcript, consistent with its role as a 'housekeeping' gene.
source: Gapdh was the most uniformly expressed transcript, consistent with its role as a 'housekeeping' gene (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observed in Figure 4B and consistent with established knowledge about housekeeping genes

claim: Ftl1 expression is highest in alveolar macrophages, where it is believed to play a role in processing iron from ingested red blood cells.
source: Ftl1 expression was highest in alveolar macrophages, as expected, where it is believed to play a role in processing iron from ingested red blood cells (McGowan and Henley, 1988).
evidence: Observed in PLISH data and referenced to prior work on Ftl1 function

claim: Ftl1 is highly expressed in Club cells.
source: Unexpectedly, Ftl1 was also highly expressed in Club cells.
evidence: Observed in PLISH data

claim: Actb expression is highest in macrophages, presumably because of its functional role in motility.
source: Actb expression was highest in macrophages, presumably because of its functional role in motility, and in AT1 cells, which must maintain a flat morphology and expansive cytoskeleton (Foster et al., 2010).
evidence: Observed in PLISH data and inferred from known function of Actb

claim: Actb expression is highest in AT1 cells, which must maintain a flat morphology and expansive cytoskeleton.
source: Actb expression was highest in macrophages, presumably because of its functional role in motility, and in AT1 cells, which must maintain a flat morphology and expansive cytoskeleton (Foster et al., 2010).
evidence: Observed in PLISH data and inferred from known AT1 cell morphology

claim: The Club cell class mapped perfectly onto the bronchial epithelium.
source: First, the Club cell class mapped perfectly onto the bronchial epithelium, while cells from the AT1 and AT2 classes were distributed throughout the alveolar compartment.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping shown in Figure 4C

claim: AT1 and AT2 cells are distributed throughout the alveolar compartment.
source: First, the Club cell class mapped perfectly onto the bronchial epithelium, while cells from the AT1 and AT2 classes were distributed throughout the alveolar compartment.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping shown in Figure 4C

claim: Rare BASCs localize precisely to the bronchioalveolar junctions.
source: The rare BASCs also localized precisely to the bronchioalveolar junctions, where they have been shown to reside by immunostaining (Kim et al., 2005) (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Observed in Figure 4C and validated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, consistent with prior work

claim: The macrophage class is primarily found inside the alveolar lumen.
source: The macrophage class was primarily found inside the alveolar lumen, and many exhibited a characteristic rounded cell shape.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping

claim: Many macrophages exhibited a characteristic rounded cell shape.
source: The macrophage class was primarily found inside the alveolar lumen, and many exhibited a characteristic rounded cell shape.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping

claim: The Otherd class of cells is enriched in pulmonary arteries and might represent endothelial or perivascular cells.
source: The Otherd class of cells was enriched in pulmonary arteries, and therefore might represent endothelial or perivascular cells.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping and inferred from anatomical location

claim: ActbHi Club cells cluster together at the bronchial terminus.
source: ActbHi Club cells clustered together at the bronchial terminus, while ActbLo Club cells populated more proximal domains (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: ActbLo Club cells populate more proximal domains of the terminal airways.
source: ActbHi Club cells clustered together at the bronchial terminus, while ActbLo Club cells populated more proximal domains (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: Two sub-classes of Club cells, defined by differential Actb expression, segregate anatomically.
source: We further observed a striking spatial segregation of the two Club cell classes.
evidence: Observed in spatial remapping shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: PLISH can integrate molecular and spatial features of single cells to generate insights that would be missed with either piece of information alone.
source: While the significance of this pattern is not immediately obvious, it emphasizes how PLISH can readily integrate molecular and spatial features of single cells to generate insights that would be missed with either piece of information alone.
evidence: Inferred from the discovery of spatially segregated Club cell subclasses

claim: PLISH specificity derives from coincidence detection, which requires two probes to hybridize next to one another for signal generation.
source: The specificity derives from coincidence detection, which requires two probes to hybridize next to one another for signal generation.
evidence: Explanation of the mechanism underlying PLISH specificity

claim: Efficient detection of low-abundance transcripts by PLISH is accomplished by targeting multiple sites along the RNA sequence.
source: Efficient detection of low-abundance transcripts is accomplished by targeting multiple sites along the RNA sequence.
evidence: Explanation of the mechanism for efficient detection

claim: Enzymatic amplification in PLISH produces extremely bright puncta.
source: Enzymatic amplification produces extremely bright puncta, and allows many different RNA transcripts to be marked with unique barcodes in one step.
evidence: Stated property of the PLISH technique

claim: PLISH allows many different RNA transcripts to be marked with unique barcodes in one step.
source: Enzymatic amplification produces extremely bright puncta, and allows many different RNA transcripts to be marked with unique barcodes in one step.
evidence: Stated property of the PLISH technique

claim: PLISH is scalable without requiring specialized microscopes, software, or computational expertise.
source: While low-plex PLISH on a handful of different genes can be valuable, the PLISH technology is also scalable, without requiring specialized microscopes (or other equipment), software, or computational expertise.
evidence: Stated property of the PLISH technique

claim: PLISH oligonucleotides and enzymes are inexpensive and commercially available from multiple vendors.
source: The oligonucleotides and enzymes are inexpensive and commercially available from multiple vendors.
evidence: Stated property of PLISH reagents

claim: H probes are the cost-limiting reagent for PLISH but can be synthesized in pools.
source: The H probes are the cost-limiting reagent, but can be synthesized in pools (Murgha et al., 2014; Beliveau et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated cost consideration with reference to pooled synthesis methods

claim: The cost of PLISH reagents amounts to $3 per gene, assuming five pairs of H probes and 20 cents for a 40mer oligonucleotide.
source: Assuming five pairs of H probes for each target RNA species, and 20 cents for a 40mer oligonucleotide, the cost of PLISH reagents amounts to $3 per gene.
evidence: Calculated cost estimate based on stated assumptions

claim: It is practical to simultaneously interrogate entire molecular systems with PLISH, such as signaling pathways or super-families of adhesion receptors.
source: It should therefore be practical to simultaneously interrogate entire molecular systems, such as signaling pathways or super-families of adhesion receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the scalability and cost-effectiveness of PLISH

claim: The high specificity and signal-to-noise of PLISH is advantageous for deep profiling, where non-specific background increases with increasingly complex mixtures of hybridization probes.
source: The high specificity and signal-to-noise of PLISH will be advantageous for deep profiling, where non-specific background increases with increasingly complex mixtures of hybridization probes (Moffitt et al., 2016c).
evidence: Inferred advantage based on PLISH properties and referenced to prior work on probe complexity

claim: PLISH has capacity for rapid, automated and unbiased cell-type classification.
source: Our initial studies demonstrate PLISH's capacity for rapid, automated and unbiased cell-type classification, and illustrate how it can complement single-cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNAseq).
evidence: Demonstrated by the multiplexed lung experiment

claim: Sc-RNAseq offers greater gene depth than in situ hybridization approaches.
source: Sc-RNAseq offers greater gene depth than in situ hybridization approaches, but it is less sensitive, fails to capture spatial information, and induces artefactual changes in gene expression during tissue dissociation (van den Brink et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison to scRNA-seq based on established knowledge and cited references

claim: Sc-RNAseq is less sensitive than PLISH.
source: Sc-RNAseq offers greater gene depth than in situ hybridization approaches, but it is less sensitive, fails to capture spatial information, and induces artefactual changes in gene expression during tissue dissociation (van den Brink et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison to scRNA-seq based on established knowledge and cited references

claim: Sc-RNAseq fails to capture spatial information.
source: Sc-RNAseq offers greater gene depth than in situ hybridization approaches, but it is less sensitive, fails to capture spatial information, and induces artefactual changes in gene expression during tissue dissociation (van den Brink et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Inherent limitation of dissociation-based methods, cited references

claim: Sc-RNAseq induces artefactual changes in gene expression during tissue dissociation.
source: Sc-RNAseq offers greater gene depth than in situ hybridization approaches, but it is less sensitive, fails to capture spatial information, and induces artefactual changes in gene expression during tissue dissociation (van den Brink et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from van den Brink et al., 2017 and Lee et al., 2015

claim: PLISH provides cytological and spatial information that is missing from sc-RNAseq.
source: PLISH provides the missing cytological and spatial information, and it is applied to intact tissues.
evidence: Stated advantage of PLISH over scRNA-seq

claim: PLISH is applied to intact tissues.
source: PLISH provides the missing cytological and spatial information, and it is applied to intact tissues.
evidence: Stated property of PLISH

claim: Multiplexed PLISH can distinguish true biological variation from technical noise and experimentally-induced perturbations.
source: Going forward, sequencing can be used to nominate putative cell types and molecular states based on the coordinate expression of 'signature genes', and multiplexed PLISH can be used to distinguish true biological variation from technical noise and experimentally-induced perturbations.
evidence: Proposed application based on PLISH capabilities

claim: Multiplexed PLISH provides the tissue context of distinct cell populations, which is essential for understanding the higher-order organization of intact systems like solid tumors and developing organs.
source: Importantly, multiplexed PLISH provides the tissue context of distinct cell populations, which is essential for understanding the higher-order organization of intact systems like solid tumors and developing organs.
evidence: Stated advantage of PLISH for understanding tissue organization

claim: In diseases like IPF where morphology and gene expression are severely deranged, histological, cytological and spatial features may be essential for making biological sense of sequencing data.
source: In diseases like IPF where morphology and gene expression are severely deranged (Xu et al., 2016), histological, cytological and spatial features may even be essential for making biological sense of sequencing data.
evidence: Inferred importance based on disease characteristics and cited reference

claim: PLISH can be combined with conventional immunostaining.
source: We have already demonstrated the combined application of PLISH with conventional immunostaining.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2C

claim: Oligonucleotide-antibody conjugates make it possible to mix and match protein and RNA targets in a multiplexed format.
source: Going one step further, oligonucleotide-antibody conjugates make it possible to mix and match protein and RNA targets in a multiplexed format (Weibrecht et al., 2013).
evidence: Referenced to prior work on oligonucleotide-antibody conjugates

claim: The generation of comprehensive, multidimensional molecular maps of intact tissues will have a fundamental impact on basic science and medicine.
source: The generation of comprehensive, multidimensional molecular maps of intact tissues, in both healthy and diseased states, will have a fundamental impact on basic science and medicine.
evidence: Speculative statement about future impact

claim: PLISH utilizes only commodity reagents.
source: PLISH utilizes only commodity reagents, so it can be scaled up inexpensively to cover many genes.
evidence: Stated property of PLISH reagents

claim: PLISH works well on conventional formalin-fixed tissues that have been cryo- or paraffin-embedded.
source: It works well on conventional formalin-fixed tissues that have been cryo- or paraffin-embedded, and can be performed concurrently with immunostaining, making it extremely versatile.
evidence: Demonstrated in experiments with both cryo and FFPE samples

claim: PLISH can be performed concurrently with immunostaining.
source: It works well on conventional formalin-fixed tissues that have been cryo- or paraffin-embedded, and can be performed concurrently with immunostaining, making it extremely versatile.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2C

claim: Murine Club cells separate into two populations that differ molecularly and segregate anatomically.
source: An unexpected discovery from this experiment is that murine Club cells separate into two populations that differ molecularly and segregate anatomically.
evidence: Discovered through multiplexed PLISH analysis shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: PLISH constitutes a novel, single cell spatial-profiling technology that combines high performance, versatility and low cost.
source: PLISH constitutes a novel, single cell spatial-profiling technology that combines high performance, versatility and low cost.
evidence: Summary statement based on demonstrated properties

claim: Because of its technical simplicity, PLISH will be accessible to a broad scientific community.
source: Because of its technical simplicity, it will be accessible to a broad scientific community.
evidence: Inferred from the use of standard reagents and equipment

claim: Proximity ligation at Holliday junctions offers a simple mechanism for the amplified detection of RNA.
source: Proximity ligation at Holliday junctions offers a simple mechanism for the amplified detection of RNA (Labib et al., 2013).
evidence: Referenced to prior work on proximity ligation

claim: Target RNAs can be tiled with H probe pairs at multiple sites, which is critical for efficient detection of low abundance transcripts.
source: Importantly, target RNAs can be tiled with H probe pairs at multiple sites, which is critical for efficient detection of low abundance transcripts (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated design principle illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Rolling-circle replication generates a long single-stranded amplicon of tandem repeats.
source: Finally, the 3' end of the right H probe primes rolling-circle replication, which generates a long single-stranded amplicon of tandem repeats.
evidence: Description of the RCA mechanism

claim: Addition of fluorescently-labeled 'imager' oligonucleotides complementary to the barcodes generates an extremely bright punctum at the site of each labeled transcript.
source: Addition of fluorescently-labeled 'imager' oligonucleotides complementary to the barcodes generates an extremely bright punctum at the site of each labeled transcript.
evidence: Description of the detection mechanism

claim: Each barcode sequence is unique, allowing puncta derived from different target RNAs to be labeled with different colors.
source: Because each barcode sequence is unique, the puncta derived from different target RNAs can be labeled with different colors (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated design principle illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: PLISH adapted protocols for antibody-based proximity ligation.
source: To implement PLISH, we adapted protocols for antibody-based proximity ligation (Söderberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Referenced to prior work on proximity ligation

claim: PLISH utilizes conventional oligonucleotides, two commercially available enzymes, and procedures familiar to molecular biologists.
source: The technique utilizes conventional oligonucleotides, two commercially available enzymes, and procedures familiar to molecular biologists.
